questions.stem: Vasco da Gama landed at which Indian port in May 1498, establishing the first direct sea route from Europe to India?
questions.explanation: Vasco da Gama reached CALICUT on 20 May 1498 and was received by the local ruler Zamorin (Samoothiri Raja). Calicut was the preeminent Malabar spice-trade port at the time. Cochin became a later Portuguese stronghold (after Zamorin's hostility drove them south in 1500). Goa was captured much later (1510) under Albuquerque. Surat became a Mughal port the Portuguese — and later the English — used in the 17th century. The 1498 Calicut landfall is the canonical date that opens modern European–Indian history.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Who among the following is credited with formulating the 'Blue Water Policy' (Cartaze system) that aimed at establishing Portuguese control of the Indian Ocean through a passport-permit regime for non-Portuguese ships?
questions.explanation: Francisco de Almeida (Viceroy 1505-09) articulated the 'Blue Water Policy' (Portuguese: 'Política do Mar Azul') — Portugal's strength lay in sea-power, not in holding territory on land; command of the sea would let them monopolise the spice trade. The complementary Cartaze system required non-Portuguese merchant ships to buy Portuguese-issued permits to trade in the Indian Ocean. Albuquerque, his successor (1509-15), pivoted to 'blue-water-plus-strategic-land-bases' — capturing Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), Hormuz (1515). Vasco da Gama was the navigator, not an administrator. Nino da Cunha moved the Portuguese capital from Cochin to Goa (1530).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem:
Arrange the following European trading companies in India in the correct CHRONOLOGICAL order of their FOUNDING (not of their arrival in India):
(i) French East India Company (La Compagnie des Indes orientales)
(ii) English East India Company
(iii) Dutch East India Company (VOC)
(iv) Portuguese Estado da Índia
questions.explanation: Correct order: (iv) Portuguese Estado da Índia — 1505 (Almeida appointed first Viceroy); (ii) English East India Company — 31 Dec 1600 (Queen Elizabeth I's charter); (iii) Dutch East India Company (VOC) — 20 Mar 1602 (Dutch States-General charter, only 15 months after the English); (i) French East India Company — 1664 (under Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Louis XIV's finance minister). Despite Dutch and English founding dates being only ~15 months apart, English is first. The Portuguese didn't have a joint-stock company structure — the 'Estado da Índia' was a royal government apparatus.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Sir Thomas Roe's diplomatic mission (1615-18) to secure trading rights for the English East India Company was sent to the court of which Mughal Emperor?
questions.explanation: Sir Thomas Roe was dispatched by James I of England to the court of JAHANGIR (r. 1605-27) at Ajmer and later Agra. Roe secured a royal firman permitting English factories at Surat and other Mughal ports — a diplomatic coup. His memoirs (published as 'The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to India') remain a primary source for Jahangir's court. Akbar died in 1605, before the mission; Shah Jahan reigned 1628-58; Aurangzeb 1658-1707 — Roe met neither. (An EARLIER English envoy, William Hawkins, had been at Jahangir's court 1609-11 without securing firm concessions.)
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The three Carnatic Wars (1744-48, 1749-54, 1758-63) decided the colonial fate of South India. Which war effectively settled the Anglo-French struggle in India, with the decisive Battle of Wandiwash?

options.option_text: First Carnatic War (1744-48), ended by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle
Second Carnatic War (1749-54), ended by the Treaty of Pondicherry
Third Carnatic War (1758-63), ended by the Treaty of Paris
A fourth war fought separately in 1780-84

questions.explanation: The THIRD Carnatic War (1758-63) — a sideshow to the global Seven Years' War — was the decisive British victory. At Wandiwash (22 Jan 1760) Eyre Coote crushed the French under Comte de Lally. The subsequent Treaty of Paris (1763) restored French factories to France but STRIPPED them of the right to fortify — thereby ending French ambitions to compete as a political power in India. The First Carnatic War saw French gains (capture of Madras) later returned via the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle; the Second was inconclusive. Option D refers to the Second Mysore War (1780-84) — different theatre.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) was fought between the forces of Robert Clive and:
questions.explanation: Plassey (Palashi in Bengali) pitted Clive against SIRAJ-ud-DAULA, Nawab of Bengal (who had captured Calcutta from the British in 1756, causing the 'Black Hole' incident). Clive's victory — aided by Mir Jafar's betrayal of Siraj — was the foundational moment of British territorial power in India. Mir Qasim was a later Nawab (installed then deposed by the British) — he lost the Battle of Buxar in 1764. Shuja-ud-Daula was Awadh's Nawab, also defeated at Buxar. Haider Ali of Mysore was an entirely different theatre (Mysore Wars 1767-1799).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Treaty of Allahabad (1765), signed between Robert Clive and the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, transferred which crucial right to the British East India Company?

options.option_text: The office of Nizamat (criminal administration) of Bengal
The Diwani (revenue collection rights) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa
Ownership of the city of Delhi
Permission to mint coins in the name of the British Crown

questions.explanation: The Treaty of Allahabad (signed after British victory at Buxar 1764) granted the Company the DIWANI of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa — the right to collect land revenue — in exchange for an annual payment of 26 lakh rupees to the emperor. This marked the TRANSITION of the Company from 'traders' to a 'territorial power' with a steady revenue source (₹30+ million annually by the 1770s). The Nizamat (criminal and police administration) was initially left with the Nawab of Bengal but became a puppet office — Warren Hastings formally combined Diwani + Nizamat under Company control in 1772. Options C and D describe events that never happened under this treaty.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which of the following European powers established its first Indian factory at TRANQUEBAR (on the Coromandel coast) in 1620 and later sold all its Indian possessions to the British in 1845?
questions.explanation: The DANISH East India Company (Dansk Ostindisk Kompagni, 1616) operated from Tranquebar (Tharangambadi, Tamil Nadu) and Serampore (West Bengal). Denmark's Indian presence was always modest — never a major political force — and after financial troubles, Denmark sold Tranquebar and Serampore to the British in 1845. The Dutch had factories further south (Nagapattinam, Pulicat) and dominated Cochin — they lost most holdings to the British by the 1780s-90s. The Swedish East India Company (1731) traded with Canton but didn't establish lasting Indian factories. The French had Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahé, Karaikal, Yanam — all retained until 1954 (de facto).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Joseph François Dupleix — who famously envisioned a French empire in India through intervention in local succession disputes — served as the Governor-General of which French Indian enclave?
questions.explanation: Joseph François Dupleix was Governor-General of French India (1742-54), based at PONDICHERRY (Puducherry). He pioneered the strategy of training sepoys on European lines and backing local claimants to the Nawabi of Carnatic and the Nizamate of Hyderabad — a tactic Robert Clive later turned against him. Dupleix was eventually recalled to France in 1754 and died in 1763 in poverty and disgrace, ironic given his Indian ambitions. Chandernagore was a French factory but never their capital. Mahé was a minor French enclave. Surat was a Mughal/English port — never French.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Battle of Colachel (1741) — a rare and decisive DEFEAT of a European colonial power by an Indian kingdom — was won by Maharaja Marthanda Varma of Travancore against which European power?
questions.explanation: Colachel (31 July 1741) was fought between Travancore and the DUTCH East India Company. Marthanda Varma's forces captured Dutch commander Captain Eustachius De Lannoy (who subsequently served as Travancore's military chief — 'Valiya Kapitaan' — and modernised its army). This battle is often highlighted in UPSC/state-PSC answer keys as the 'first European defeat by an Indian kingdom' — though Portuguese defeats by local Zamorin forces had occurred earlier in the 16th century. After Colachel, Dutch power in the Malabar never recovered; by 1795 their last holdings fell to the British.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Bombay was transferred to the English East India Company in 1668 by which English monarch, having received the islands as part of the dowry of his Portuguese queen?
questions.explanation: When Charles II of England married Catherine of Braganza (daughter of King John IV of Portugal) in 1661, the Portuguese dowry included Bombay (7 small islands). Charles II, finding the islands hard to administer, leased them to the EIC in 1668 for a nominal rent of £10 per year. The EIC rapidly developed Bombay as a fortified port, and by the late 17th century it had eclipsed Surat as the Company's western headquarters. Elizabeth I died in 1603 — before the dowry event. James I was on the throne when Sir Thomas Roe went to Jahangir's court but died in 1625. George III came much later (r. 1760-1820).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem:
Which of the following is the CORRECT chronological order of the establishment of EIC 'Presidency' headquarters in India?
(i) Madras  (ii) Bombay  (iii) Calcutta  (iv) Surat
questions.explanation: Correct order: (iv) SURAT was the first EIC factory (1613, after Thomas Best's 1612 Swally battle) — served as the western headquarters initially. (i) MADRAS was founded 1639-40 when Francis Day obtained Madrasapatnam from the Vijayanagara viceroy — Fort St. George built there. (ii) BOMBAY was leased to EIC in 1668 (dowry from Charles II's Portuguese marriage), displacing Surat as the western headquarters by 1687. (iii) CALCUTTA (Fort William) was established 1690 by Job Charnock. So: Surat → Madras → Bombay → Calcutta. Knowing the decade of each presidency is a high-ROI memorisation.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Who was appointed as the FIRST Governor of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773, and subsequently became the first Governor-General of Bengal (with supervisory authority over Madras and Bombay)?
questions.explanation: Warren Hastings was already Governor of Bengal when the Regulating Act 1773 elevated the Bengal governorship to 'Governor-General of Bengal' — with authority to oversee (but not directly govern) Madras and Bombay presidencies. The post carried a 4-member council (initially hostile to him under Philip Francis). Hastings served 1773-85. Clive's role was earlier — he was Governor of Bengal twice (1757-60, 1765-67) but predated the Regulating Act and never held the 'Governor-General' title. Cornwallis (1786-93) succeeded Hastings and pushed the Permanent Settlement. Wellesley (1798-1805) pushed Subsidiary Alliances.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Afonso de Albuquerque — often called the 'founder of the Portuguese empire in the East' — captured which three strategic cities during his governorship (1509-15)?
questions.explanation: Albuquerque's strategic trifecta: GOA (1510, from Bijapur — made Portugal's Asian capital), MALACCA (1511, from the Malay Sultanate — controlling the Strait and spice route east), HORMUZ (1515, controlling the Persian Gulf trade). He tried and failed at Aden. Calicut was never conquered — only unsuccessfully besieged. Macau was acquired in 1557, decades after his death. Colombo came to Portuguese control later through negotiation with Kotte. Knowing GOA-MALACCA-HORMUZ as Albuquerque's signature conquests is the canonical answer.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Pitt's India Act of 1784 established the Board of Control to oversee the EIC in London. This Board was chaired by which official of the British Government?
questions.explanation: Pitt's India Act (1784) created a DUAL system: the EIC retained commercial control, but political/military decisions came under a Board of Control composed of 6 Cabinet members, headed by a 'President of the Board of Control' — a Cabinet-rank minister. This post, reorganised by the Government of India Act 1858 after the 1857 Revolt, became the 'Secretary of State for India' reporting to Parliament. So answer B is correct. The PM did NOT directly chair the Board; the King had a ceremonial role but not operational chairmanship. The Archbishop has no role here — pure distractor. later the Secretary of State for India.
questions.subject: History

_fixes.was: A Cabinet Minister (later the Secretary of State for India)
